Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a clear prompt for getting help configuring our family photo archive. the family is Leah and Omar Haddad, their two teenagers, and Leah’s mother, who lives nearby. we are trying to bring several years of pictures together without turning this into a complicated project that only one person understands. the archive is for family photos and home videos, not a public collection or a professional studio. the useful answer should explain a practical setup in ordinary language and connect the choices to the way we actually use the files.

we have about 18,000 photos and 600 short videos from 2008 through 2024. most are JPEGs from phones and cameras, with some RAW files from Omar’s camera and a few scanned prints from Leah’s mother. the material is currently split across two portable drives, phones, and a stack of SD cards. filenames are inconsistent, and some phones may have exported copies of photos that are already on a drive. we want to avoid deleting anything during the first import. several older pictures have dates or location details in their metadata, but the scanned prints often do not. please ask for a way to keep original files and their available metadata, identify likely duplicates for review, and arrange browsing by year without pretending every image has a reliable date.

at home we already have a small network storage box in the study, a desktop computer that stays on most evenings, and one 4 TB external drive. the storage box is reachable from the home network, but it sometimes restarts after updates, so it might not be available when an import is due. there is no second storage box and we have not chosen a photo-management application. don’t assume a particular brand of NAS or an app; if a specific app matters, explain what feature we would need rather than making the whole plan depend on an unmentioned product. the photos are private family material, and we prefer that the main archive remain in the house.

please make the import steps safe and understandable for Leah and Omar, who have different levels of computer experience. if the network storage box is reachable when we start an import, copy the files to it and verify the copied files before treating that batch as archived. if it is not reachable, do not try a remote connection or pretend the import succeeded; keep that batch on the computer or external drive as a temporary staging copy, and move it to the storage box only after it becomes reachable and the copy can be checked. explain both branches, including what happens to the originals during each branch. we want an orderly process for adding future phone and camera files too, not just a one-time migration.

remote access is a separate concern. Leah’s mother sometimes asks to see recent pictures when she is away from home, and she said, “I don’t need every old picture on my phone, just a few from the weekend.” however, we do not want the archive itself exposed remotely. describe how the setup should handle that request while remote access stays disabled, and distinguish a family-selected set of pictures from access to the whole archive. don’t change the remote setting just because someone requests a few images. the selected pictures can be shared separately, but the main archive should stay local. if discussing any way of sharing them, keep the archive’s remote-access policy and the separate sharing action clearly distinct.

use this configuration excerpt as part of the prompt and explain the settings in the proposed guidance without changing the literal values:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 7
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

please have the answer cover what the seven-day retention value means for this local copy, and clarify that it is not the same as a complete long-term backup. we only have the one external drive today, so describe its role accurately and don’t call it a second independent storage system. we have not decided whether to buy more storage. mention that the current capacity and future growth should be checked against the size of the collection, without inventing a capacity estimate or selecting equipment for us. explain what the name “local-copy” identifies, and don’t treat it as a security feature by itself.

organize the requested guidance into a short overview, a staged import and verification workflow, and practical notes about browsing, duplicates, metadata, and the external drive. include a numbered section with these points:
1. what to prepare before the first import, including a simple inventory of the drives and cards;
2. how the reachable and unavailable storage-box cases change the import steps;
3. how to review possible duplicates and handle files with missing dates;
4. how to add later phone and camera batches and check that they were copied.

keep the explanation useful for a household rather than assuming a technical administrator. separate what the configuration says from any advice about the workflow, and don’t imply that the current setup has already been tested. end with a substantive paragraph about the next decisions the family would need to make, including whether the external drive is enough for their needs and how they want to share selected pictures with Leah’s mother while the archive remains local. do not write a sales pitch or a conclusion that claims the archive is fully protected.", "output": "Create practical, plain-language guidance for configuring a private family photo archive for Leah and Omar Haddad, their two teenagers, and Leah’s mother, who lives nearby. The archive is for family photos and home videos, not a public collection or professional studio. Explain the setup in a way that is understandable to family members with different levels of computer experience, and relate the recommendations to how the family uses its files.

The collection contains about 18,000 photos and 600 short videos from 2008 through 2024. Most files are JPEGs from phones and cameras; there are also some RAW files from Omar’s camera and scanned prints from Leah’s mother. Files are currently spread across two portable drives, phones, and SD cards. Filenames are inconsistent, and some phone exports may duplicate files already on a drive. Avoid deleting anything during the first import. Explain how to retain original files and available metadata, identify likely duplicates for review, and browse by year without assuming that every image has a reliable date. Some older pictures have date or location details in their metadata, while scanned prints often do not.

The family already has a small network storage box in the study, a desktop computer that stays on most evenings, and one 4 TB external drive. The storage box is reachable on the home network but sometimes restarts after updates, so it may not be available when an import is due. There is no second storage box, and the family has not selected a photo-management application. Do not assume a particular NAS brand or app. If a specific application matters, explain the feature needed rather than making the plan depend on an unmentioned product. The photos are private family material, and the family prefers to keep the main archive in the house.

Provide a safe, understandable import workflow for both the initial migration and future additions. Make the storage-box availability condition explicit:
- If the network storage box is reachable when an import starts, copy the files to it and verify the copied files before treating that batch as archived.
- If it is not reachable, do not attempt a remote connection or imply that the import succeeded. Keep that batch on the computer or external drive as a temporary staging copy, then move it to the storage box only when the box is reachable and the copy can be checked.

Explain what happens to the originals in each case. Include an orderly process for adding future phone and camera files, not just a one-time migration.

Remote access is a separate concern. Leah’s mother sometimes asks to see recent pictures while away from home and said, “I don’t need every old picture on my phone, just a few from the weekend.” Keep the archive’s remote access disabled. Explain how the family can handle a request for a few selected pictures separately from access to the whole archive. Do not change the remote setting because someone requests a few images. If you discuss sharing, distinguish the separate sharing action from the policy for remote access to the archive.

Use this configuration excerpt and explain its settings without changing any literal values:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 7
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"

Explain what the seven-day retention value means for this local copy and clarify that it is not a complete long-term backup. Describe the single external drive accurately; do not call it a second independent storage system. The family has not decided whether to buy more storage. Note that current capacity and future growth should be checked against the collection’s size, but do not invent a capacity estimate or select equipment for the family. Explain what the name “local-copy” identifies and do not present the name itself as a security feature.

Organize the guidance into a short overview, a staged import and verification workflow, and practical notes on browsing, duplicates, metadata, and the external drive. Include a numbered section covering:
1. What to prepare before the first import, including a simple inventory of drives and cards.
2. How the reachable and unavailable storage-box cases change the import steps.
3. How to review possible duplicates and handle files with missing dates.
4. How to add later phone and camera batches and check that they were copied.

Keep the explanation appropriate for a household rather than a technical administrator. Distinguish what the configuration says from workflow advice, and do not imply that the setup has already been tested. End with a substantive paragraph about decisions the family still needs to make, including whether the external drive is enough for their needs and how they want to share selected pictures with Leah’s mother while keeping the archive local. Avoid a sales pitch or a conclusion claiming the archive is fully protected."}]
